lead: A CSS rule is a selector plus a block of declarations, and a page usually holds many rules that fight over the same element. CSS defines a winner with the cascade: importance first, then specificity, then document order. Specificity is a four-part counter — inline style, ids, classes and attributes, elements — compared left to right. Every page you have ever seen uses this: the blue header on IRCTC, the red error text under a UPI form, the hover colour on a button. Get the counters right and the page looks as designed; get them wrong and you spend an evening wondering why nothing changes.
prereq: You need chapter 2.1 for the link and style elements, and chapter 2.2 for the content elements you will style.

sections.h3: Anatomy of a rule and its units

blocks.text: A CSS rule has two parts. The selector chooses the elements; the declaration block says what to change. Each declaration inside the braces is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon: p { color: #333; font-size: 16px; }. Here p is the selector, color and font-size are properties, #333 and 16px are values.

Write the semicolon after every declaration, the last one included. A missing semicolon between two declarations glues them into one invalid declaration; the browser drops that one declaration and continues with the rest of the block. The last declaration may legally omit the semicolon before }, but write it anyway so that adding a new line later cannot break the block. Comments sit between /* and */, may span lines, and cannot be nested. Property names are lowercase.
A length needs a unit; only 0 may drop it. The common units:

head: Unit
Measured against
One unit is
rows: one CSS pixel, a fixed size
the element's own font-size (the parent's, when set on font-size)
the parent's value for that property
1% of the parent's value for that property, so 50% of the parent's width is half the parent's width
1% of viewport width, 1% of viewport height

blocks.text: Inline. <p style="color: green;">text</p> puts declarations in a style attribute on one element. No selector is written; they apply to that element only, and they beat any selector except !important. Useful for a one-off; bad for a site, because the style cannot be reused or cached.
Internal. A <style> element inside <head> applies to the whole document but only to that one page. Handy for a single page or a quick test.

External. <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/site.css"> in the head fetches a separate file. The browser caches it and reuses it on every page that links it. This is the normal choice for a real site: one file, many pages, and the CSS is fetched in parallel with the HTML.

@import url("print.css"); at the top of a stylesheet pulls in another file. It works, but it is slower. The browser cannot discover the imported file until it has downloaded and parsed the file that imports it — an extra round trip — and rendering may be held up meanwhile. A <link> is found as soon as the head is scanned, so prefer it.
A selector pattern is matched against the document tree. Learn these by name; examiners ask for them by name.

items: [type="text"] — attribute, elements whose attribute has that value.
h1, h2 — grouping, one declaration block for both.
div p — descendant, any p inside a div at any depth.
h2 + p — adjacent sibling, the p straight after an h2.
h2 ~ p — general sibling, every p after an h2 under the same parent.
a:hover, input:focus, li:first-child, li:nth-child(2n), p:not(.note) — pseudo-classes: a state or a position, written with one colon.
p::before, p::after, p::first-line — pseudo-elements: a part of an element, written with two colons.

blocks.text: A pseudo-class adds nothing new to the tree; it filters. :nth-child(2n) counts from 1, so 2n means items 2, 4, 6 and :nth-child(2n+1) means 1, 3, 5. ::before and ::after generate a box only when the rule also sets content, for example content: "→";.

When several rules match one element, the cascade decides in this order: importance (!important first), then origin, then specificity, then document order — among equals, the later rule wins. Only the winning value for a property is applied; the other declarations are not merged.

Specificity is four counters, compared left to right, never added: (1) is there an inline style attribute, (2) how many ids, (3) how many classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, (4) how many elements and pseudo-elements. * counts nothing. So #intro p is (0,1,0,1) and p.note is (0,0,1,1).

Inheritance is separate from the cascade. Text properties such as color, font-family and line-height pass from parent to child when the child sets nothing. Box properties — margin, padding, border, width — do not pass down.
!important after a value lifts that declaration above normal ones, including an inline style. It is a last resort: a few of them are fine, a file full of them means the selectors were written badly.

figure.caption: Read the counters left to right: the id rule beats the class rule in the ids column, so the text is blue; the style attribute wins in the first column, so it turns green; !important is checked before any counter, so the red rule finally wins.

spec.aria: A table of specificity counters: #intro p is 0,1,0,1, p.note is 0,0,1,1, the style attribute is 1,0,0,0; below, three steps paint blue, then green, then red after !important.

examples.question: Two rules match the same paragraph: #intro p { color: blue; } and p.note { color: red; }. Which colour is painted? Then style="color: green" is added to that element — which colour now? Finally the red rule alone is marked !important, the attribute still says green. Which colour now?
steps: Counter for #intro p: 0 inline styles, 1 id, 0 classes, 1 element = (0,1,0,1).
Counter for p.note: 0 inline styles, 0 ids, 1 class, 1 element = (0,0,1,1).
Compare position by position: first counter 0 = 0, second counter 1 > 0, so the id rule wins. The text is blue.
Adding the style attribute creates a third entry, (1,0,0,0). Its first counter is 1 against 0 for both rules, so it wins immediately. The text turns green.
Marking the red rule !important changes the order of the cascade, not the counters. Importance is checked before specificity, and the style attribute is not important, so red wins.
Final sequence of colours: blue, then green, then red.
examples.answer: The paragraph is blue, then green after the inline style, then red once the red rule is marked !important.
examples.check:
a = (0, 1, 0, 1)  # #intro p
b = (0, 0, 1, 1)  # p.note
c = (1, 0, 0, 0)  # style attribute
for t in (a, b, c):
    print(*t)
print(*max(a, b, c))  # normal cascade winner
print(*b)             # winner once p.note is !important

traps: Adding the four counters into one number. (0,1,0,1) and (0,0,1,1) both sum to 2, but the id rule wins. Compare left to right, position by position.
Forgetting that a pseudo-class sits in the third counter (with classes and attributes) while a pseudo-element sits in the fourth. a:hover is (0,0,1,1), not (0,0,0,1).
Thinking an inline style always wins. It beats ids and classes, but a declaration marked !important in a normal stylesheet beats it.
:nth-child(2n) counts from 1 among all siblings, so it selects the 2nd, 4th, 6th child — not the 0th, 2nd, 4th. Write 2n+1 for odd items.

A missing semicolon between two declarations glues them into one invalid declaration; the browser drops that one declaration and continues with the rest of the block. The last declaration may legally omit its semicolon before }, but write it anyway. !important must come before the semicolon: color: red !important;.

quiz.q: List the three ways of attaching CSS to an HTML document.
quiz.a: Inline style attribute on the element; internal <style> element in the head; external file linked with <link rel="stylesheet">.
(0,1,2,0): no inline style, one id, one class plus one pseudo-class, no elements.

quiz.q: Why is a linked stylesheet preferred over @import?
quiz.a: The <link> is seen while the head is parsed and the file is fetched in parallel. An @import is only discovered after the importing file has been downloaded and parsed, so it costs an extra round trip and can delay the first paint.

quiz.q: A paragraph sits inside a div and has class="note". The matching rules are p { color: blue }, div p { color: red } and .note { color: green }. What colour is the text, and why?
quiz.a: p = (0,0,0,1), div p = (0,0,0,2), .note = (0,0,1,0). The class rule wins on the third counter, so the text is green.
For n = 0, 1, 2, … the formula gives 1, 4, 7, 10, so the 1st, 4th, 7th … items. Counting starts at 1, so the first item matches.

quiz.q: A student says p.note and #intro p are a tie because each scores 2. Explain what is wrong.
quiz.a: The four counters are not digits of one number and are not summed; they are compared column by column from the left. On the id counter p.note has 0 and #intro p has 1, so #intro p wins before the later columns are even looked at.

quiz.q: Why does color pass from a parent to its child while margin does not?
quiz.a: Inheritance is decided per property by the CSS specification. Text properties inherit so that text keeps one consistent look down the tree. Box properties do not inherit, because every child repeating the parent's margins and padding would make layout impossible to control.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CSS adds cascade layers (@layer), which group rules into named layers that outrank plain specificity, and the :has() selector, which styles a parent based on what it contains. Container queries let a component respond to the width of its own box rather than the viewport, which suits reusable cards. Large teams often write styles next to components in JavaScript, the CSS-in-JS style used in React and Angular projects (see Unit 5, Front-End Frameworks: React and Angular). Preprocessors such as Sass add variables and nesting and compile down to plain CSS. Search for “CSS cascade layers”, “container queries” and “CSS-in-JS” to go further.
